title: Tally Board
context: Grade 4. An adult sees marks on a chart. What is actually being learnt is that a tally records each answer the moment it comes, so each answer gets one mark and none is left to count later, and that bundles of five make a count quick to read. The page defines tally marks as vertical bars, when the fifth mark of each bundle is drawn across the four before it, and one question in the exercise that follows is worded as though a list of favourites could say which children prefer one flavour to another. This tool draws the fifth mark across every time, and asks how many more children chose one thing than another.

writeup.why: Record each answer with one tally mark as it comes, draw every fifth mark across the four before it, read a tally in fives, and compare the rows of a tally chart.
writeup.look: A tally chart drawn as a board, with a belt of answer cards along its top, a pen for each row, and a compare bar at its foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Tally Board' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the marks drawn, or the rows read, against what this phase holds, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each mark is drawn or each row's number drops into its column. The second is fixed at the cards on the belt or the rows on the chart. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The belt runs along the top of the working area, 1072 by 76 at 64,212. Answer cards, each 110 by 60 with the answer's name on it, arrive from the right one at a time and wait at the belt's left end. The tally chart fills the middle, up to six rows, each 50 tall with 4 between, from 300 to 620. It has three columns: the name, 200 wide at 64; the tally marks, 640 wide at 264; and the number, 120 wide at 904. Tapping a row draws one short upright mark in it, deep blue, 6 wide and 40 tall, 14 from the mark before. The waiting card turns face down and moves one place along the belt, so a marked card shows face down. Every fifth tap in a row draws its mark in vermilion across the four standing, from the foot of the first to the top of the fourth. The bundle closes with a soft ring, and the next mark starts a new bundle 22 further along. A row holds up to eight bundles and four single marks. The counting finger rides above whichever row is tapped. It lights each bundle in turn, writing five, ten, fifteen over the bundle it has just passed, then lights each single mark in ones. The row's number then drops into the number column in amber. The total cell stands beside the foot of the number column, 110 by 50 at 1034,570, and adds the number column in reddish purple. It is labelled answers, or children when each child gave one answer. The compare bar lies along the foot, 840 by 100 at 64,630, in two lanes 46 tall. Two rows dragged into it are laid one under the other, bundle under bundle and mark under mark from the same left edge. The marks one row has beyond the other are banded sky blue and counted. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count is asked for. A word pad carries the chart's own row names and the words bundle, more, fewer and in all. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A mark is never drawn anywhere but in a row, and never without its card turning. The pen never draws a fifth mark upright. Where the child draws a mark by hand, it stays exactly as drawn, and the pen's own bundle is drawn beside it rather than over it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the tally chart the child made from the belt, every fifth mark drawn across, with its number column, its total and the two rows they compared.

phases.win: the belt empties, every card is turned, and the marks in the rows match the cards
phases.does: taps the row for each card as it arrives and watches its mark drawn and the card turn over
phases.goal: one mark is drawn for each answer as it comes, so each answer gets one mark and none is left to count later
phases.says: Where does this answer go? One mark for each answer.
phases.check: Away from the screen: tally the colours of ten pencils, one mark as each comes out of the tin.
phases.feels: one card, one tap, one mark, and a marked card lies face down on the belt
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, send groups to the school gate or a window with clipboards for ten minutes. They draw one mark for each car, bike, bus and person walking as it passes. Back in class, read out a list of answers one at a time, and have the class mark each as it comes. Ask why marking as it comes is safer than going back through the list once for each name.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which row does this answer belong to? Second rung, the phase's: has every card been turned over? Third rung: the belt is cut to four cards and two rows, and the child marks each as it comes. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: counting one pet at a time feels tidy, and every pass through the list is a fresh chance to skip one.
wrong.move: goes back through the list once for each pet, misses a cat on the way, and gives the cat row one mark.
wrong.screen: the belt runs the six cards again one at a time, and each card turns face down as its mark is redrawn in its row. The cat row comes to two marks beside the child's one, and the cat card that was passed over lifts a little as it turns.

wrong.why: copying from a list means keeping a place with the eye, and a place is easy to lose.
wrong.move: copies a list of nine answers into the chart and loses one, so the bus row has three marks where the list has four.
wrong.screen: the list is laid on the belt as nine cards, and each turns face down as its mark is drawn. The bus row comes to four marks, and the running count comes to nine, one for each card. The child's row of three stays beside it.

phases.screen: an empty tally chart with a row for each answer and a belt of answer cards along the top
phases.soWhat: One mark is drawn for each answer as it comes, so each answer gets one mark and none is left to count later.

phases.win: the mark falls across the four, the bundle closes with a ring, and the next mark starts a new bundle
phases.does: draws the fifth mark across the four, then carries on marking into a new bundle
phases.goal: every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, making a bundle of five
phases.says: Four marks are standing. Where does the fifth one go?
phases.check: Draw tally marks for twelve. How many marks lie across?
phases.feels: four marks standing and the fifth lying across them, closed off and easy to see as five
phases.hands: Draw four upright marks on the board and ask where the fifth goes. The page's first sentence on tally marks calls them upright strokes, and its next sentence lays every fifth one across the four, as its worked chart does. Teach the two sentences together, and call each one a mark: four short uprights, and the fifth drawn across them from corner to corner. Then show seventeen together, bundle by bundle, leaving a small gap before each new bundle.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many marks are standing in this bundle? Second rung, the phase's: where does the fifth mark go? Third rung: the row is cut to four standing marks, and the child draws the fifth. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: every mark so far has stood upright, and a fifth looks like just one more of the same.
wrong.move: draws the fifth mark upright beside the four, so the row is a line of single marks with no bundles.
wrong.screen: the child's upright fifth mark stays where it was drawn. Beside the row the pen draws the same five again, four standing and the fifth laid across them in vermilion, and the bundle closes with its ring. The two stand side by side.

wrong.why: the crossing mark looks like a line drawn to close a group, not like a mark that is counted.
wrong.move: draws five upright marks and then crosses them with a sixth, so each bundle holds six.
wrong.screen: the counting finger reads the child's first bundle mark by mark and reaches six, writing it over the bundle. The pen then draws a bundle of five beside it, four standing and one across, and the finger reads that one as five.

wrong.why: the next mark goes beside the last one, and a gap looks like wasted room.
wrong.move: starts the next mark inside the closed bundle, with no gap, so two bundles run together.
wrong.screen: the pen redraws the row with a small gap before each new bundle, and the child's row stands above it with its marks run together. The finger then reads the pen's row in fives.

phases.screen: a row with four marks standing and a fifth answer card arriving on the belt
phases.soWhat: Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, making a bundle of five.
phases.concept: The fifth mark crosses the four

phases.win: each bundle lights as it is counted and the row's number drops into the number column
phases.does: runs the counting finger along each row, counting the bundles in fives and then the single marks
phases.goal: a tally is read by counting its bundles in fives and then the marks left over
phases.says: Count the bundles in fives. Then count on the marks left over.
phases.check: A tally shows three bundles and four more marks. How many is that?
phases.feels: the bundles go by in fives, and the last few marks are counted on in ones
phases.hands: Hand out strips with tallies drawn on them, and have pairs read each one aloud: five, ten, fifteen for the bundles, then sixteen, seventeen for the marks left over. Ask what each bundle is worth before anyone counts. Then give a long row and ask why counting one mark at a time is slower, and easier to lose.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many bundles are there? Second rung, the phase's: what is each bundle worth? Third rung: the row is cut to one bundle and two marks, and the child counts them. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: the four uprights are what stand out, and the mark lying across looks like a line through them.
wrong.move: counts each bundle as four, reading only the upright marks, so four bundles and three read as nineteen.
wrong.screen: the counting finger lights each bundle whole, the fifth mark with it, and writes five, ten, fifteen, twenty over the bundles. It then counts on the single marks to twenty-three. The child's nineteen stays in the slot.

wrong.why: counting in fives has a rhythm, and the rhythm carries on past the last bundle.
wrong.move: carries on counting in fives over the single marks, so two bundles and three read as twenty-five.
wrong.screen: the finger lights the two bundles with five and ten, then stops. It lights each single mark in ones, eleven, twelve, thirteen, and the row's number drops in as thirteen beside the child's twenty-five.

wrong.why: counting in ones feels safe, and a long row of marks has nothing in it to hold the place.
wrong.move: counts a long row one mark at a time, loses the place, and counts one bundle twice, so three bundles and one read as twenty-one.
wrong.screen: the finger lights each bundle once, leaving a small tick over it as it passes, and says five, ten, fifteen, then sixteen for the single mark. No bundle is lit twice. The child's twenty-one stays beside the sixteen.

phases.screen: a finished tally chart with its number column empty and the counting finger waiting
phases.soWhat: A tally is read by counting the bundles in fives and then the marks left over in ones.

phases.win: the marks beyond the shorter row light, their count lands in the answer slot, and the total fills
phases.does: lines two rows up on the compare bar, counts the marks one row has beyond the other, then totals the chart
phases.goal: how many more is the smaller count taken from the larger, and the total adds every row
phases.says: How many more chose this one? Line the rows up and look at what is left.
phases.check: Nine chose kites and six chose tops. How many more chose kites?
phases.feels: two rows lined up from the same edge, and the difference sitting in plain view at the end of the longer one
phases.hands: Put two rows of a class tally side by side and ask how many more chose one than the other. Line them up from the same edge and count what the longer row has left. One exercise question is worded as how many children like one flavour more than another. A list of favourites cannot say which children prefer what, so ask how many more children chose it, and take the smaller count from the larger. Add a chart up for the number of children only when each child gave one answer, and say so whenever the class does it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which row is longer? Second rung, the phase's: what is left when the shorter row runs out? Third rung: the compare bar is cut to one bundle against one bundle and two marks, and the child counts what is left. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: the question names cricket first, and cricket's number is the one the eye finds.
wrong.move: answers how many more children chose cricket than kabaddi with sixteen, the number who chose cricket.
wrong.screen: the two rows are laid in the compare bar, bundle under bundle. The kabaddi lane runs out at nine, and the seven marks the cricket lane has beyond it are banded sky blue and counted. The child's sixteen stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the question names two rows, and joining two numbers has always meant adding them.
wrong.move: adds the two rows for how many more, giving twenty-five for sixteen and nine.
wrong.screen: the compare bar lines the two rows up, and only the marks beyond the shorter one are banded. Seven is written on the band, and the child's twenty-five stays beside it.

wrong.why: every chart added so far came to the number of children, because each child gave one answer.
wrong.move: adds a chart in which each child named two games, and calls the forty answers forty children.
wrong.screen: the total cell adds the number column and is labelled answers. The belt's cards are then grouped by the child who gave them, two to each child, and the children come to twenty.

phases.screen: a tally chart with its numbers written, a question card, and the compare bar at the foot
phases.soWhat: How many more is the smaller count taken from the larger. The rows add up to the children when each gave one answer.
phases.concept: A tally chart and how many more

writeup.delight: The second phase, whenever a bundle closes. For a moment the five marks of that bundle lift and fan out into the five answer cards that made them, face up, each with its name. Then they fold back down into the bundle. On a finished row a tap on any bundle does the same. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the tally chart stands empty, a row for each answer with its name written, and the belt holds its answer cards face up at the right. On the second one row stands with four upright marks in it, and a fifth card waits at the head of the belt. On the third a finished chart stands with its number column empty and the counting finger resting at the left of the first row. On the fourth a chart stands with its numbers written, a question card sits in the slot, and the compare bar waits at the foot with both lanes empty. The running count at the top left holds the marks drawn or the rows read against what this phase holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the card at the head of the belt, or the fifth card, or the counting finger, or the compare bar, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where the answer goes. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any list of answers on the belt and up to six rows, with the counting finger, the compare bar and the total all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on one mark for each answer, the fifth mark drawn across the four, reading a tally in fives, and comparing the rows of a tally chart for how many more and how many in all.

Free play. Any answers on the belt, with the finger and the compare bar open.

Every answer marked once, every bundle closed, and every row read in fives.

observations.why: One tap draws one mark and turns one card, so no answer is marked twice or passed over.
observations.soWhat: A tally records each answer the moment it comes, so each answer gets one mark and none is left to count later.
observations.observe: Every card on the belt turned over as its mark was drawn, and the marks in the rows came to the cards on the belt.

observations.why: Crossing the four closes a group of five that the eye takes in at once.
observations.soWhat: Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, so a tally falls into fives.
observations.observe: The fifth mark in every bundle lay across the other four, and the next mark started a new bundle.

observations.why: Each bundle holds five, and the marks after the last bundle are fewer than five.
observations.soWhat: A tally is read in fives for the bundles, then in ones for the marks left over.
observations.observe: The finger said five, ten, fifteen over the bundles, then counted the single marks in ones.

observations.why: The two rows were lined up from the same edge, bundle under bundle.

source_tool.description: A tally chart fills the stage as a board with a row for each answer and three columns: the name, the tally marks and the number. Answer cards arrive one at a time along a belt at the top of the board, and the child taps the row each card belongs to, which draws one short upright mark in that row and turns the card over, so every answer is marked once and none is missed. On every fifth tap in a row the pen draws its mark across the four marks already standing, corner to corner, and the bundle closes with a soft ring; the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap. A counting finger reads any row in fives: it lights each bundle in turn and says five, ten, fifteen, then lights the marks left over one at a time, and writes the row's number in the third column. A compare bar lines two rows up one under the other, bundle under bundle, so the marks one row has beyond the other stand out, and they are counted to answer how many more. A total control adds the number column when each child gave one answer.
source_tool.art_direction: A chalk tally board with a belt / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a desk with a drawn class and a heap of answer slips, a ruled table, a tally board with a belt of answer cards, pictograph boards with a title strip and a key card, symbols that fold down their middle, a small route map, a tray of picture stamps, and a key dial.
Every pictograph carries a title strip at its top and a key card beside it from the first frame. A title or key still to be filled is an outlined blank, never a space left out.

Every symbol in one pictograph is one plain picture drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same edge in every row or column, so a row's length is its count of symbols. A face, a kite, a cup, a tree or a bus; no letter, sign or mark ever stands in for a picture.

When the rows of a pictograph name colours, each row's symbols, whole or half, are drawn in that row's colour, and the key's symbol in plain grey. Otherwise every symbol in one pictograph, the key's included, is drawn in one colour.

A half symbol is the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it. It always comes last in its row. Halves are the only part of a symbol ever drawn, and only on a key that halves into whole things.
A tally mark is one short upright line. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, corner to corner, and the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap.
A pictograph drawn up the page stacks its symbols from the bottom. Its side is left unnumbered, or numbered only in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted, and never in symbols.

The count of symbols and the number they stand for are never written in the same place: symbols are counted at the top left of the canvas, and a row's number is written at the end of its row with its unit.
The sum of every row is written under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, and never beside a single row.
A row, a symbol or a mark is told apart by its name or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a tally mark, a symbol, a number, a band or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and the fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that counts in fives cannot afford a bundle whose closing mark has to be hunted for. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in every row, is green, except where the rows are told apart by colour: there every symbol in a row is that row's own colour, red, green, blue, yellow or purple, and the key's symbol is plain grey, a grey used for nothing else, because it stands for a symbol of any colour. What a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, the number written beyond a row's end, the numbers in a table, the numbers a side ruler writes in the data's own units, what half a symbol stands for, and what a key leaves over, is amber. A total of every row, and a thing that a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share, are reddish purple. The row a question asks about, and the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another, are marked by a pale sky blue band behind the symbols or marks. Every table rule, row line, belt, bracket, outlined blank and card border is near-black chrome, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. All of that holds in greyscale, because a fifth mark lies across and not upright, a half symbol is the left half of the whole, a row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

placement.where: After groups have tallied what passed the school gate on clipboards, and before the printed tally chart is made. The tool is what turns each answer card over as its mark is drawn, so a missed or doubled answer is seen, and what closes every fifth mark across the four, which a hurried hand often leaves standing.

answer_key.rule: A tally mark is drawn for each thing counted, as it comes. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, making a bundle of five, and the next mark starts a new bundle. A tally is read by counting the bundles in fives and then the marks left over in ones. A tally chart sets each name beside its marks and its number. How many more is found by taking the smaller count from the larger, and when each child gave one answer, the numbers add up to the number of children.
answer_key.wrong: The belt runs the answer cards past again one at a time, each mark is redrawn as its card turns, and the counting finger rereads the row bundle by bundle, saying five for each. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: As each answer comes, draw one mark in that pet's row.
Dog, cat, dog, rabbit, dog, cat gives dog a mark three times, cat twice and rabbit once.
Six answers made 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 marks, one for each child.
items.answer: Dog 3 marks, cat 2 marks and rabbit 1 mark
items.question: Six children say their favourite pet, one at a time: dog, cat, dog, rabbit, dog, cat. Make a tally for each pet.
items.checkpoint: One mark is drawn for each answer as it comes, so each answer gets one mark and none is left to count later.
items.misconception: Going back through the list once for each pet and missing or repeating an answer, instead of marking each answer once as it comes.

steps: Draw four marks, then draw the fifth mark across the four. That is one bundle of five.
Two more bundles make 10 and then 15.
Two more single marks make 16 and 17.
items.answer: Three bundles of five and 2 more marks
items.question: Show 17 in tally marks.
items.checkpoint: Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, making a bundle of five.
items.misconception: Drawing the fifth mark as one more standing mark, so the marks never fall into fives and must be counted one by one.

steps: Count on the single marks in ones: 21, 22, 23.
items.question: A row shows four bundles and 3 single marks. How many is that?
items.checkpoint: Count the bundles in fives, then add the marks left over.
items.misconception: Counting each bundle as 4, because four marks stand upright, and missing the mark drawn across them.

steps: Read each row in fives: cricket 16, football 13, kabaddi 9 and badminton 10.
Kabaddi has the smallest count. For how many more, take the smaller count from the larger: 16 - 9 = 7.
Each child chose one sport, so add every row: 16 + 13 + 9 + 10 = 48.
items.answer: Kabaddi was chosen least; 7 more children chose cricket than kabaddi; 48 children in all
items.question: A tally chart of favourite sports shows cricket three bundles and 1 mark, football two bundles and 3 marks, kabaddi one bundle and 4 marks, and badminton two bundles. Each child chose one sport. Which sport was chosen least, how many more children chose cricket than kabaddi, and how many children are there in all?
items.checkpoint: How many more is found by taking the smaller count from the larger.
items.misconception: Answering 16, the number who chose cricket, when the question asks how many more chose cricket than kabaddi.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Eight answers come in: tea, milk, milk, juice, tea, milk, juice, milk. How many marks go in each row?
A tally chart holds 9 marks in all, one for each answer. How many answers were collected?
How many bundles of five and how many single marks show 14?
Draw tally marks for 20. How many marks are drawn across?
items.final_answer: 4, one in each of the four bundles of five

items.question: A row shows three bundles and 1 single mark. How many is that?
A tally of vehicles at a gate shows cars two bundles and 2 marks, buses one bundle and 3 marks, and bikes three bundles and 4 marks. Write each count.
A tally chart of fruit chosen shows guava two bundles and 1 mark, papaya one bundle and 2 marks, and orange three bundles. How many more children chose orange than papaya?
items.final_answer: 8 more, because orange shows 15 and papaya 7

items.question: A tally chart of snacks shows samosa three bundles and 3 marks, idli two bundles and 4 marks, poha one bundle and 1 mark, and dhokla two bundles and 2 marks. Each child chose one snack. Which snack was chosen least, and how many children were asked in all?
items.final_answer: Poha, chosen by 6; 50 children in all, because 18 + 14 + 6 + 12 = 50

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: brings answer cards one at a time along the top of the board
draws one mark in the row an answer belongs to and turns its card over
draws every fifth mark in a row across the four before it
reads a row in fives, then the marks left over in ones
writes each row's count beside its marks
lines two rows up, bundle under bundle, to show how many more
adds the number column when each child gave one answer

teaching_notes: Tally something real before the tool is opened: groups stand at the school gate or a window for ten minutes and mark each car, bike, bus and person walking as it passes. The page defines tally marks as vertical bars. Say instead that each thing counted is one short mark, and that every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, so a bundle is five and a count is read in fives. The page's own worked tally and every chart in the chapter draw the fifth mark that way. Tally chart is used from the first worked Example on and never defined: it is a chart with each name beside its tally marks, and usually its number. One question in the exercise that follows is worded as though a list of favourites could say which children prefer one flavour to another. It cannot. Ask how many more children chose one than the other, and find it by taking the smaller count from the larger. A tally chart's total is the number of children only when each child gave one answer, so say so whenever the class adds one up.
generation_prompt: Build a tally tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tally chart fills the working area as a board with up to six rows and three columns: the name, the tally marks and the number. A belt along the top brings answer cards one at a time; tapping the row a card belongs to draws one short upright mark in that row and flips the card face down. On every fifth mark in a row the pen draws a line across the four marks already standing, corner to corner, and the bundle closes with a soft ring; the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap. A counting finger reads a row by lighting each bundle in turn with a spoken five, ten, fifteen, then each single mark, and writes the row's count in the number column. A compare bar at the foot lines two chosen rows up, one under the other, bundle under bundle, and lights the marks one row has beyond the other. A total control adds the number column. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Tap the row each answer belongs to. Draw one mark for each answer. Draw the fifth mark across the four. Count the bundles in fives. Then count the marks left over. Line two rows up to find how many more.
